text:
Garry Kasparov was a Soviet-born chess prodigy who became the youngest-ever world chess champion at age 22, holding the title for six years and establishing himself as the highest-rated player in history with a peak Elo of 2851. His career was defined by a fierce rivalry with Anatoly Karpov, spanning five matches in which Kasparov retained the title three times, including a dramatic 1985 victory that coincided with the end of the Cold War. Following a contentious dispute with FIDE, Kasparov broke away from the organization in 1993, leading a split in the world championship with Karpov remaining as the FIDE champion. He subsequently defended his title under the Professional Chess Association and later retired in 2005 to pursue writing and political activism.
Post-retirement, Kasparov became a prominent political dissident in Russia, criticizing President Vladimir Putin and organizing opposition movements. His views on democracy, human rights, and international affairs extended globally, including commentary on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the war in Ukraine, and the Armenian genocide. He also maintained an active presence in the chess community, coaching future champions like Magnus Carlsen and Fabiano Caruana, while engaging in exhibitions and promoting chess education. Kasparov's legacy encompasses not only his unparalleled dominance in chess but also his influence as a public intellectual and his contributions to the development of computer chess and opening theory.
